Very few vocations had robust data for a day-road group, but will be recognized in the text above the figure as such. When numerous vocations are shown on a day-road graph, they do not all contribute equally to the speed distribution for the source type, as some have more vehicles than others, and that will be the major determiner of proportional contributions. In Figure 48, we show the speed distribution for each vocation individually that makes up the combination-unit short-haul source type. Only drayage trucks on weekdays traveling on urban other roads and transfer trucks on weekdays on both urban road types had robust data based on the hourly analysis (refer to Appendix A). Likely due to these robust data, these distributions do not have sharp peaks that jump out in the graphs, and their distributions are sometimes hidden behind others, but we do see a 55–60-mph peak for transfer trucks on urban roads on weekdays, for example. Parcel delivery trucks appear to drive faster on urban roads on weekends compared to other vocations, while food distribution trucks tend to drive slower than other vocations. Drayage vehicles display a 60-mph peak on urban freeways on weekends, while agricultural trucks from CE-CERT favor a 60–65-mph peak. Line-haul trucks and cement mixers behave similarly when driving on rural freeways. Interestingly, beverage delivery vehicles tend to drive faster on other roads compared to most vocations, but slower more often than other vocations on freeways. 59 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. Figure 48. Vocational speed bin distributions for combination-unit short-haul vehicles Figure 49 displays the vocation-specific distributions within the single-unit short-haul source type. On urban freeways, street sweepers tend to drive slightly faster than freeway work trucks but slower than most other vocations based on the peak of their speed distributions. Freeway work trucks peak on the 50-mph midpoint bin, and street sweepers on the 55-mph bin, while utility and linen delivery trucks peak around 60 mph and parcel and warehouse delivery near 65 mph. Drayage trucks can be seen with a very shallow peak near 60 mph and spending more time in 20–30-mph and 70–85-mph speed bins compared to other vocations on urban freeways on weekdays. Food and parcel delivery trucks on urban other roads on weekdays were the only vocations with robust data; however, most vocations follow a similar broad, low-speed peak for this category, with parcel delivery and snow plows peaking slightly faster at 10 and 20 mph, respectively, while street sweepers and freeway work trucks spend more time than other vocations at the 5-mph midpoint bin.
